summary.text: A weather radar locates precipitation, works out how it is moving and estimates whether it is rain, snow, hail or something else.
It grew out of World War II, when radar operators found weather echoes masking enemy targets, and surplus radars were turned on precipitation soon after the war.
Modern Doppler radars track how fast particles move as well as where and how intense precipitation is, which helps show the structure of storms and their potential for severe weather.

facts.label: Wartime origin
facts.value: Weather echoes masked enemy targets in World War II

items.prompt: Radar wasn't built to watch the weather. How did meteorologists come to use it?

options.label: Astronomers adapted it to track planets
Wartime operators saw storms cluttering screens
TV stations designed it for weather shows
Airlines built it to locate runways

items.explain: In World War II, weather caused echoes that masked targets; scientists studied the effect, and surplus radars were used for precipitation after the war.

items.prompt: An older radar shows where rain is falling and how heavy it is. What can a Doppler radar add?

options.label: The colour of the clouds
The temperature of each raindrop
How fast the particles are moving
The exact count of hailstones

items.explain: Doppler radars track the relative velocity of particles in the air, in addition to position and intensity.

items.prompt: As Hurricane Carla neared Texas in 1961, how did a TV reporter help get people to accept a huge evacuation?

options.label: He showed the live radar image of the storm
He flew a plane right into the storm's eye
He read out a list of past hurricane deaths
He filmed the waves rising along the coast

items.explain: Dan Rather broadcast live from a radar site, laying a traced map over the radar display to show Carla's size and eye, which helped people accept evacuating.

items.prompt: In 1973 a Doppler radar followed a tornado through its whole life. What did it pick up before the tornado touched the ground?

options.label: A burst of hail at ground level
A sudden gap in the rain
A sharp drop in air temperature
Rotation high up in the cloud

items.explain: Researchers found a mesoscale rotation in the cloud aloft before touchdown, now called the tornadic vortex signature.

items.prompt: A radar sends out microwaves polarized both horizontally and vertically. What does this mainly add?

options.label: A longer range for spotting storms
Better clues to whether it's rain or snow
A clearer picture of the ground
Protection from wartime jamming

items.explain: Dual polarization increases the information on precipitation type, such as rain versus snow.

items.prompt: A radar only measures how strongly falling water reflects its signal. What lets it turn that into how hard it's raining?

options.label: A relation tying reflectivity to rainfall rate
A count of the drops passing the dish
A thermometer mounted on the dish
The colour of the returned echo

items.explain: Marshall and Palmer's work on drop sizes led to the Z-R relation, which links a given radar reflectivity to the rate rainwater is falling.
